parsed_answer.content:
The Executor Framework, introduced in Java 5 via the `java.util.concurrent` package, provides a standard, decoupled mechanism for running tasks asynchronously in concurrent applications. Before its introduction, Java developers relied on raw `Thread` instantiation and manual thread management, which directly coupled task submission with thread creation and execution lifecycle. Raw thread creation introduces severe scalability bottlenecks: every new thread consumes significant OS resources, including memory allocation for native thread stacks (typically 1MB per thread), kernel scheduler context switching overhead, and garbage collection pressure from transient thread objects. The Executor Framework solves these structural issues by abstracting away the mechanics of thread creation and management through the `Executor` and `ExecutorService` interfaces.

At the core of the framework is the separation of task submission from execution policies. Developers define units of work using `Runnable` or `Callable` interfaces and submit them to an `ExecutorService`, which manages a pool of worker threads. This architecture relies heavily on internal blocking queues to buffer incoming tasks when concurrency limits are reached, preventing the system from spawning an unbounded number of threads that would otherwise trigger `OutOfMemoryError` exceptions or system thrashing. By reusing a pre-allocated pool of worker threads, the framework amortizes the expensive cost of thread creation across thousands of asynchronous tasks, maximizing CPU cache locality and maintaining predictable throughput under heavy production loads.

rows: Unbounded creation; prone to OutOfMemoryError and OS thread exhaustion.
Bounded pooling via core and maximum pool sizes with controlled queue capacities.
No built-in hooks; requires manual tracking, joining, and interruption logic.
Comprehensive lifecycle methods (shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination, isTerminated).
Fire-and-forget via Runnable; requires complex inter-thread signaling to return values.
First-class return value support using Future<V> and Callable<V>.
Requires manual use of java.util.Timer or complex sleep-loop constructs.
Native delayed and periodic execution support via ScheduledExecutorService.

items: Worker Thread Reuse: The ThreadPoolExecutor maintains a pool of worker threads that continuously poll an internal BlockingQueue for new tasks, drastically reducing JVM-to-OS context switching overhead.

Future and Callable Integration: Unlike Runnable, Callable allows tasks to return computed results and throw checked exceptions, which are safely encapsulated within a Future handle for asynchronous synchronization.

Graceful Shutdown Mechanics: The ExecutorService lifecycle allows applications to drain existing queued tasks before termination or forcibly interrupt running operations via shutdownNow(), preventing thread leaks during container redeploys.

parsed_answer.content: Production Gotcha: Avoid using convenience factory methods like Executors.newCachedThreadPool() or Executors.newFixedThreadPool() in high-throughput enterprise applications. newCachedThreadPool creates an unbounded thread pool (maximum pool size of Integer.MAX_VALUE), which can easily spawn thousands of threads under bursty traffic and crash the JVM with an OutOfMemoryError. Similarly, newFixedThreadPool utilizes an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, risking heap exhaustion if the ingestion rate of tasks persistently outpaces execution speed. Always instantiate ThreadPoolExecutor directly with bounded queues and explicitly defined RejectionExecutionHandlers.

title: Explain the Executor Framework. Why is it better than creating raw threads?
